claims.text: Sec. 1671(a) adds 50 U.S.C. 3373(l)(5): 'Each briefing under this subsection shall include, for the period covered by the briefing, details on any unidentified anomalous phenomena intercepts conducted by the North American Aerospace Defense Command or the United States Northern Command', with summaries of 'the number, location, and nature of such intercepts' and 'a description of the procedures and protocols followed during the intercepts, including any data collected or analyzed during such intercepts.'

Sec. 1671(a) new subparagraph (C) requires the Director of AARO to 'inform the appropriate congressional committees of any failure by the North American Aerospace Defense Command or the United States Northern Command to provide timely information on unidentified anomalous phenomena intercepts' - an anti-stonewalling clause written against two combatant commands by name.

Sec. 1671(b), note '50 USC 3373 note', imposes a retrospective look-back: the first briefing after enactment 'shall include details on any unidentified anomalous phenomena intercepts conducted by the North American Aerospace Defense Command or the United States Northern Command not previously provided that occurred during the period beginning on January 1, 2004, and ending on the last day of the period otherwise covered by the briefing.'

Sec. 1672(a) repeals sec. 413 of the IAA for FY2022 (50 U.S.C. 3373a). Sec. 1672(b) rewrites 50 U.S.C. 3373(f)(1)(A) to read: 'The Director of National Intelligence and the Secretary of Defense shall jointly require that each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense with data relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena makes such data available immediately to the Office in a manner that protects intelligence sources and methods.' The added qualifier 'in a manner that protects intelligence sources and methods' is new and was not in the repealed provision.

Sec. 1673(a), note '50 USC 3373 note', requires the Director of AARO within 180 days of enactment to 'make an accounting of security classification guides that apply to information used for reports and investigations of unidentified anomalous phenomena' and permits issuance of 'a consolidated security classification matrix for programs relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena to provide a resource for programs that support or may be affected by investigations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena.' Sec. 1673(b) requires the results to be included in the 2026 annual report under 50 U.S.C. 3373(k).
PL 119-60 was 'Approved December 18, 2025.'

Sec. 1673's premise is that no one currently has a map of which classification guides control UAP information across the government - four years after AARO was created by statute. The authorisation of a 'consolidated security classification matrix' for 'programs relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena' is an admission in enacted law that a plurality of such programs exists and that their classification authorities are not centrally known. Reasoning: Congress does not order an accounting of guides that are already inventoried.

The 1 January 2004 look-back date in sec. 1671(b) is the month of the USS Nimitz / 'Tic Tac' encounters. Congress selected a start date that reaches back to the earliest incident in the modern public record rather than to AARO's creation, indicating the committees believe intercept records from that period exist and have not been briefed. Reasoning: no other event anchors that specific date in UAP legislative history.
P.L. 119-60 was approved 18 December 2025 and originated as S. 1071; its Subtitle E consists of Secs. 1671, 1672 and 1673.
Sec. 1671(b) requires the first NORAD/NORTHCOM intercept briefing to cover intercepts 'during the period beginning on January 1, 2004.'
Sec. 1673 requires an accounting of security classification guides applying to UAP reports and investigations within 180 days, and permits a consolidated security classification matrix.
P.L. 119-60 contains zero instances of 'eminent domain', 'non-human', 'legacy program' or 'reverse engineer'.

desc: The FY2026 NDAA shows the disclosure agenda reduced to housekeeping and the oversight machinery beginning to be dismantled. P.L. 119-60, approved 18 December 2025, contains a Subtitle E of Title XVI headed 'Matters Relating to Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena' with three sections. Sec. 1671 amends 50 U.S.C. 3373(l) to require that AARO's briefings include details of any UAP intercepts conducted by NORAD or United States Northern Command, with the first such briefing required to reach back over intercepts 'that occurred during the period beginning on January 1, 2004' — Congress choosing the year of the Nimitz encounters as its retroactive floor. Sec. 1672 repeals Sec. 413 of the IAA FY2022, codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373a, and rewrites the data-availability clause so that intelligence and DoD components must make UAP data available 'immediately' to AARO. Sec. 1673 orders the AARO Director within 180 days to make an accounting of the security classification guides applying to UAP reporting and permits issuance of a consolidated security classification matrix — a direct probe at the classification architecture itself. What the Act does not contain is as important: zero instances of 'eminent domain', 'non-human', 'legacy program' or 'reverse engineer'; no Review Board; and, critically, no renewal of the Sec. 1687 or Sec. 7343 funding limitations. Those were one-year restrictions on funds authorised by the FY2024 Act. They were not renewed in FY2025 and were not renewed here, so the statutory bar on funding undisclosed UAP special access programmes has now lapsed for two consecutive authorisation cycles. The Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2026 that rides in Division F contains no UAP provisions at all.

claims.text: S. 2296, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, was signed into law on 18 December 2025 as Public Law 119-60; it passed the Senate on 10 October 2025.
The conferenced FY2026 NDAA contains three UAP-related provisions, all of which modify the existing All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office framework.

One provision requires the Pentagon to brief lawmakers on operations since 2004 involving UAP intercepts conducted by NORTHCOM and NORAD, and directs the AARO director to supply Congress with briefings and data on the "number, location, and nature" of such intercepts.
The same provision requires details about the procedures and protocols followed during those intercepts, "including any data collected or analyzed during such intercepts."
A second provision directs AARO to account for UAP-related security classification guides that apply to information used for reports and investigations of such phenomena.
A third provision eliminates duplicative reporting requirements and streamlines federal agencies' processes for providing relevant data and information to the Pentagon for AARO's investigations.

dossier.narrative:
S. 2296 passed the Senate on 10 October 2025 and became P.L. 119-60 on 18 December 2025. Three UAP provisions made the conferenced text, all of them modifications to the existing AARO framework rather than new authorities.

The first amends the AARO mandate to require the director to supply Congress with briefings and data on UAP intercepts conducted by U.S. Northern Command and the North American Aerospace Defense Command going back to 2004 — specifically the "number, location, and nature" of such intercepts, together with the procedures and protocols followed, "including any data collected or analyzed during such intercepts." The 2004 start date is not arbitrary; it is the year of the USS Nimitz/USS Princeton encounters off southern California. That a statutory obligation was needed in 2025 to get NORTHCOM and NORAD intercept data in front of Congress establishes that, for twenty-one years, the commands responsible for defending North American airspace were not routinely providing it — not to Congress, not to AARO, and not to the scientific community. Christopher Mellon, the former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence who now chairs the Disclosure Foundation's board, has made precisely that point publicly: the United States operates some of the world's most advanced sensor systems, and what those systems capture about anomalous incursions has not been reaching oversight.

The second provision directs AARO to account for the UAP-related security classification guides that apply to information used in reports and investigations of the phenomena. This is the provision an analyst should mine. Security classification guides are the operative documents of concealment: they are what tells a program office which facts are classified at what level and for how long, and they are signed by an original classification authority. Disclosure Foundation officials, Mellon among them, have argued in public that DoD classification guides have been applied inconsistently with executive order standards and have been used to suppress material that was previously unclassified. An accounting of those guides would produce a list of instruments, custodians and dates. Whether AARO produces it, and whether the accounting is delivered classified, is the next measurable event.

The third provision consolidates duplicative reporting requirements and streamlines how federal agencies provide data and information to the Pentagon for AARO's investigations. Streamlining is double-edged: it reduces friction for AARO, and it reduces the number of separate documents Congress receives.

Against that, consider what was excluded. Rep. Eric Burlison (R-MO) submitted the UAP Disclosure Act of 2025 as an amendment to the FY2026 NDAA in late August 2025. It would have prohibited the destruction or alteration of UAP records, created a UAP Records Collection at the National Archives, established an independent UAP Records Review Board, and required public disclosure of UAP records within twenty-five years absent a presidential certification of a clear national security reason for delay. It failed in the House. On the Senate side the same architecture was offered as S.Amdt. 3111 to S. 2296. Neither survived. The UAP Disclosure Act has now been excluded from three consecutive defense authorization bills despite bipartisan Senate backing associated with Schumer, Rounds and Gillibrand, and Liberation Times has reported that sources attribute the FY2026 failure specifically to Senator Mitch McConnell.

The records-destruction prohibition is the provision whose repeated exclusion should be read hardest. It is cheap, non-controversial on its face, and imposes no disclosure burden — it merely freezes the evidentiary record in place. Its removal, three cycles running, from a bill that Congress has enacted for more than six decades without fail, is a fact about the removers. The precedent for why it matters is documentary and sixty years old: GAO found in 1995 that the administrative records and outgoing message traffic of Roswell Army Air Field for the relevant period were destroyed with no indication of by whom or under what authority (see gao-nsiad-95-187). A statutory bar on destruction is the one measure that would prevent the 1995 finding from recurring, and it is the measure that keeps not passing.

Jordan Flowers, executive director of the Disclosure Foundation — the rebranded UAP Disclosure Fund — characterized the three enacted provisions as "a meaningful, if incremental, step toward transparency and oversight," and noted that two of them mirror recommendations Mellon and his team had promoted for years. That is the accurate reading: the FY2026 NDAA moved the oversight perimeter a few feet and left the custody question untouched.
openQuestions: What are the exact section numbers of the three UAP provisions in P.L. 119-60, and what deadlines and classification levels do they attach?
Does the classification-guide accounting have to be delivered unclassified, or may it be delivered entirely in classified annex?
Why 2004 as the start date for the NORTHCOM/NORAD intercept look-back, and who chose it?
Did the FY2026 NDAA renew, allow to lapse, or silently supersede the FY2024 funding limitation on UAP-related special access programs?
Who specifically moved to strike the records-destruction prohibition in conference, and is there a written record of the objection?
Has AARO produced any deliverable under any of the three provisions as of the date of this dossier?
dossier.whatItIs: The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, S. 2296 of the 119th Congress, signed into law on 18 December 2025 as Public Law 119-60. It carries three UAP-related provisions affecting AARO. It does not carry the UAP Disclosure Act, which was excluded for the third consecutive year.
dossier.whyImplicated: The FY2026 NDAA is the clearest available measurement of what Congress can and cannot pass on this subject. What survived is procedural: briefings, an inventory of classification guides, and reporting consolidation. What died — again — was every provision with teeth: records preservation, an independent Review Board, eminent domain over privately held recovered material, and mandatory declassification timelines. The pattern is now three cycles deep and consistent in kind: the disclosure architecture is introduced in the Senate with bipartisan leadership sponsorship, and it is removed in or around conference. One surviving provision is unusually revealing on its own terms — a directive that AARO account for the UAP-related security classification guides governing its own reports and investigations. A classification guide is a written instrument with an author, a date, and an original classification authority. Congress asking for an inventory of them is Congress conceding it does not know how many exist or who wrote them.
